name: Facial Action Coding System

lead: The Facial Action Coding System (FACS) is a scientific framework that breaks every visible facial movement into numbered 'action units', each tied to the contraction or relaxation of particular muscles. Psychologists Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen published it in 1978, building on earlier work by the anatomist Carl-Herman Hjortsjo.[1]

For people working on their appearance it provides exact language for expression: how a genuine smile differs from a polite one, which muscles lift the brows, and what makes a face look warm, tired or tense. That vocabulary is used in discussions of smile training, facial exercise and photo or video presence.

paras: FACS is a coding manual, not a routine. Trained coders watch footage and score which action units appear and how strongly (A trace to E maximum). Appearance-minded people borrow its terms, for example the Duchenne smile, which adds the muscle around the eye to the muscle that lifts the lip corners, to analyse their own expressions in photos and video.[1]

There is no physical risk. The system describes visible movement rather than the degree of muscle activation, and full coding needs a 500-plus-page manual and certification, so informal use of its terms is a loose approximation of the real method.[1]

angle.text: FACS supplies precise terms for expressions, so people can describe and compare their own smiles and resting expressions. Learners use it as a map of which muscle groups produce which look.

lead: The Facial Action Coding System (FACS) is an anatomically based method for describing facial movements by their visible appearance. Each basic movement is an action unit (AU) linked to one or more facial muscles, and movements whose muscular basis was not specified are called action descriptors.[1] It was adopted and published by Paul Ekman and Wallace V. Friesen in 1978, drawing on the Swedish anatomist Carl-Herman Hjortsjo's 1969 work, and was updated in 2002 with Joseph C. Hager.[1]

In looksmaxxing and appearance discussions FACS is a reference vocabulary. It lets people name exactly what an expression is doing, such as the eye-muscle involvement that separates a Duchenne smile from a social smile, which supports smile analysis, facial-expression practice, and the study of how animated or posed faces read to others.[1]
Beyond appearance, FACS is used in psychology, pain assessment in people who cannot speak, infant and animal expression research, computer facial animation and automatic expression recognition.[1]
infobox: Action unit (AU), intensity A to E[1]

paras: FACS classifies facial movement by what is visible. Each action unit corresponds to the contraction or relaxation of one or more muscles, and intensity is rated from A (trace) to E (maximum), with modifiers for side and symmetry.[1]

Coding is done manually by trained coders using a manual of more than 500 pages; certification comes from passing a test, and accurate annotation is recommended to involve at least two independent certified coders.[1]

Researchers use FACS to distinguish smile types, to measure pain in people who cannot describe it (including older adults with Alzheimer's disease), and to code infant expressions (Baby FACS, by Harriet Oster, for ages 0 to 2). Versions exist for chimpanzees, macaques, dogs, horses, cats and other animals.[1]

In animation, action units serve as weights for blend shapes in computer facial animation, and computer-vision researchers have worked on automatic FACS recognition, limited by a shortage of manually coded training data.[1]

The system does not provide biomechanical information about how strongly a muscle is activated, and coding currently depends on trained experts. Action descriptors are less precisely defined than action units.[1]
No studies found on FACS as an appearance intervention. FACS itself is used as a measurement tool in research studies, for example in pain and emotion-recognition research.[1]
